screens.title: Set Up Your Game Dev Environment & First C++ Program
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will build the minimal, reliable workspace that lets C++ code become a runnable program. We’ll clarify two essential roles: the compiler, which translates your human-readable code into machine instructions, and the IDE, which organizes your files and runs the compiler for you. You will see a short terminal-style demo that compiles a simple greeting program and we’ll intentionally create a couple of common mistakes so you learn to read compiler messages. This foundation matters because game development relies on fast, predictable builds and confident debugging. By the end you’ll have a working main. cpp, know how to compile it with g++ or the MinGW toolchain on Windows, and be comfortable locating and fixing the typical errors beginners make. Along the way I’ll show why header inclusion like iostream is required, what main() must look like, and how the linker produces the final executable. Let’s begin by mapping the tools, then we’ll create your first program and run it so you know your environment is ready.

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: A correct environment and basic compile-run loop turn code into an executable, which is the first step toward building games reliably.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Get Started
Setting Up Your Game Dev Environment
Tools, compilation flow, and your first working C++ program for game development.
In this lesson
Install and configure a minimal cross-platform toolchain, understand compiler and linker roles, and run a first C++ program so your development loop is working.
Why this chapter is essential
Game development demands fast iteration. A stable compile-and-run workflow lets you test features quickly and debug with confidence before adding engines or graphics.
Key Takeaway

Set up VS Code with MinGW or use GCC/Clang on macOS/Linux. Compile main.cpp into an executable to confirm your toolchain works.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Visual roadmap
Install tools
Write code
Compile & run
Explore Key Topics
Compiler vs IDE — Roles and why both are needed.
First program — main(), iostream, and output to console.
Common errors — missing semicolon, case sensitivity, and PATH issues.
Coming up: a terminal-first demo that compiles and runs main.cpp, plus intentional errors to practice reading compiler messages.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will perform four concrete skills vital to starting game development in C++. First, you will explain the roles of an IDE and a compiler in plain language and know why each tool is necessary for building executables. Second, you will set up a basic development environment suitable for beginners: Visual Studio Code with MinGW on Windows, or GCC/Clang on Mac O S and Linux. Third, you will write, compile, and execute a simple console program that prints a friendly message; this validates your toolchain and proves you can go from source to executable. Fourth, you will identify and correct common early compilation errors, like forgetting semicolons or using the wrong capitalization for main, and you will read error lines to locate the problem. Each objective includes practice you can perform immediately so you gain confidence. These skills ensure that when you later add libraries or game engines, your foundation remains solid and you can focus on gameplay rather than toolchain problems.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Validation Tasks
Quick validation checklist

screens.title: Why C++ is used for Game Development
screens.narratorSegment: C++ is a common choice for high-performance games because it gives programmers direct control over memory and an efficient path to machine instructions. In practice this means game systems like physics, rendering, and audio can be written to use memory deterministically and avoid unnecessary copies. For you as a beginner, that translates into code that can run faster and integrate tightly with game engines. A concrete example: a collision system that iterates millions of objects per frame benefits from C++ performance and predictable allocation. A common misconception is that C++ is only for experts; while it has powerful features, you can start with a small subset—basic functions, simple data structures, and clear ownership rules—before using advanced features. Another contrast: higher-level languages trade some speed for safety and easier syntax, which is fine for tools or rapid prototypes. The takeaway is to start with readable, well-structured C++ and focus on learning compilation and debugging before optimizing. That foundation lets you later adopt engine-specific systems with confidence. How might knowing memory behavior change how you design a game loop? Why C++ is used for Game Development means c++ provides the performance and control needed for game engines; begin with simple constructs and learn the compile-run cycle first.. In practical terms, performance, memory control, and hardware access explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Why C++
Definition
C++ gives explicit control over memory layout and low-level operations, enabling high-performance systems needed for many games.
Example
A physics loop processing many objects per frame benefits from predictable allocations and fast loops in C++, reducing frame-time spikes.
Common misconception
Many believe C++ is only for experts. Start small: simple main(), basic IO, and small functions before using heavy abstractions.
Why this matters for game dev
  • Deterministic memory helps avoid frame drops and fragmentation.
  • Close-to-metal performance lets engines render and simulate more each frame.
  • Interop with game engine APIs often expects C++ binaries and interfaces.
Key Takeaway

Start with readable, well-structured C++ to build confidence, then learn performance techniques relevant to game loops and engine integration.

screens.title: Compiler, Linker, and IDE — Roles Defined
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the distinct roles of compiler, linker, and IDE prevents confusion when builds fail. The compiler reads your C++ source files, checks syntax, applies preprocessing directives, and generates object code. Think of it as translating your recipe into machine fragments. The linker then takes those object files plus necessary library code and combines them into a single executable your OS can run. Without the linker, separate object files remain isolated pieces. An IDE is the environment that helps you edit files, run the compiler and linker, and debug. For example, Visual Studio Code running a terminal command like g++ main. cpp -o mygame. exe automates invoking the compiler and then the produced binary can be run. A common beginner mistake is trying to run source files directly instead of the compiled executable; the compiler must be present and reachable in PATH. Another mistake is ignoring linker errors that indicate missing functions from other object files or libraries. Fixing these means confirming compilation succeeds for all translation units and linking required libraries. How will you check whether compilation or linking failed next time you see an error?

keyIdea.title: Pipeline summary
keyIdea.text: Compiler: source to object. Linker: object + libraries to executable. IDE: workspace that runs these tools for you.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Build Pipeline
Roles
Compiler: checks syntax, runs preprocessor directives, and emits object code for each translation unit.
Linker: combines object files and libraries into a runnable executable file.
IDE: provides editor, build automation, and debugging tools so you can run the compiler and linker easily.
Common mistake
Attempting to run source code directly or ignoring linker messages. Always confirm which step failed by checking compiler output versus linker output.
Concrete example
Using g++ to compile and link in one step: the compiler produces object code and the linker creates an executable when you run a command like g++ main.cpp -o mygame.exe. If the compiler reports a syntax error, fix it; if the linker reports an undefined reference, ensure all required object files or libraries are included.
Tip

Use the IDE terminal to run compiler commands so you can see both compilation and linking messages in one place.

screens.title: Your First C++ Program
screens.narratorSegment: Now we will study a minimal C++ program that prints a greeting. This example uses the standard input-output header and a main function that returns zero to indicate success. Read the code first, then I will explain each part and why it is required. Notice the preprocessor directive that includes iostream and the use of the std::cout object with the insertion operator to send text to the console. The endl manipulator inserts a newline and flushes output so you see the message immediately. A common beginner error is omitting the semicolon at the end of the output line; that produces a syntax error during compilation. Another is writing Main or MAIN instead of main—the entry point must be lowercase. Use this sample as your first file named main. cpp. After you type it, save and compile. The code is compact and portable across platforms if you have a working toolchain. What output do you expect when this runs, and what would a missing semicolon error look like in the compiler output? Your First C++ Program means include iostream, define int main, output via std::cout, end with return 0; to signal successful execution.. keyIdea.title: Minimal program
keyIdea.text: Include iostream, define int main, output via std::cout, end with return 0; to signal successful execution.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › First Program
Source code (save as main.cpp)
<#include <iostream>>

int main() {
  std::cout << "Hello, Game Devs! Let's build something amazing!" << std::endl;
  return 0;
}
This compact program includes the iostream header, defines main where execution starts, prints a message, and returns zero to indicate success.
Line-by-line explanation
  • Preprocessor include: brings declarations for std::cout and std::endl into the translation unit.
  • int main(): required entry point for the program; returns an int to signal status.
  • std::cout << ...: sends the string to standard output; std::endl adds a newline and flushes.
  • return 0;: signals successful termination to the operating system.
Key Takeaway

This minimal program confirms your toolchain and introduces core syntax: includes, main, output, and return codes.

screens.title: Compilation Process: Source to Executable
screens.narratorSegment: Compiling C++ is a multi-step process that transforms source files into an executable. First, the preprocessor handles directives like include; it inserts header contents so the compiler sees declarations. Next, the compiler proper parses and type-checks the code, reporting syntax and semantic errors and producing assembly or object code. After that an assembler converts assembly to machine-level object files. Finally, the linker resolves references across object files and libraries and produces the final executable file that the operating system can run. A concrete example: when you run g++ main. cpp -o mygame. exe, the toolchain performs these phases, often in one command. Beginners often confuse which phase reported an error. If you see a syntax error mentioning a line in your source, that’s from the compiler phase. If you see undefined reference errors during linking, the compiler produced object code but the linker could not find needed functions in the linked objects or libraries. Practice reading which phase produced the message so you know whether to edit source, add a missing object file, or include a library. What change would you make if the linker reports an undefined reference to a function you implemented in another file?

keyIdea.title: Phase checklist
keyIdea.text: Preprocess → compile → assemble → link. Read error messages to identify which phase failed before fixing the issue.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Compilation Steps
1. Preprocessing
Handles #include and macro expansion so the compiler sees full declarations.
2. Compilation
Parses code, type-checks, and produces assembly or object code while reporting syntax errors.
3. Assembling
Converts assembly into machine-level object files.
4. Linking
Combines object files and libraries into an executable; resolves external references.
Practical check
Run one-step commands like g++ main.cpp -o mygame.exe to perform all phases; inspect output to see which phase reported errors. If the linker fails, ensure all object files or required libraries are supplied.
Misconception

An error message doesn't always mean the compiler is broken. It usually indicates a specific phase found an issue you can fix in source or build configuration.

screens.title: Terminal Demo: Compile and Run
screens.narratorSegment: We will walk through the terminal commands that compile and run your program. Use the g++ command when your toolchain provides it. A common single-step command on many systems is g++ main. cpp -o mygame and then run the program with./mygame on Mac O S/Linux or mygame. exe on Windows. On Windows with MinGW you might run g++ main. cpp -o mygame. exe and then./mygame. exe from the integrated terminal. If the compiler is not found, the error messages will say the command is not recognized; that usually means the compiler is not installed or not on PATH. When compilation fails, read the line number and message. If it reports a missing semicolon, open the file at the specified line and add the semicolon. If linking reports undefined references, ensure you included all needed source files or libraries. This terminal-first practice makes the build pipeline concrete and reproducible. Try copying the exact commands into your terminal to validate the setup and note what the output says when the run succeeds versus when an error occurs. Terminal Demo: Compile and Run means compile with g++ main.cpp -o mygame (or mygame.exe) and run the produced executable; check path if g++ is not found.. In practical terms, commands to compile and execute your first program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Run commands
keyIdea.text: Compile with g++ main.cpp -o mygame (or mygame.exe) and run the produced executable; check PATH if g++ is not found.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Terminal Demo
Commands to try
Copy these into your project terminal to compile and run the program you saved as main.cpp.
g++ main.cpp -o mygame
./mygame

# On Windows with MinGW
g++ main.cpp -o mygame.exe
./mygame.exe

# Single-step with chaining (Linux/macOS)
g++ main.cpp -o mygame && ./mygame
If the terminal says command not found, confirm MinGW or GCC/Clang is installed and that g++ is in your PATH environment variable.
Example output
When the compile and run succeed you will see the greeting printed, for example: Hello, Game Devs! Let's build something amazing!
Check your work

If you do not see output, check the compile step for errors and ensure you ran the produced executable, not the source file.

screens.title: Common Beginner Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often encounter a short set of recurring errors when compiling C++. Three that appear most frequently are: missing semicolon, wrong case for main, and missing include for iostream. The missing semicolon produces a compiler syntax error that usually points to the line following the mistake. Fixing it is as simple as adding a semicolon at the end of the statement. Using Main with a capital letter or misspelling means the linker or runtime will not find the required entry point; the program may compile but fail to link or run properly. Forgetting to include iostream results in an error that std::cout is not declared; the compiler will flag the unknown identifier. When you read the error, note the file and line number, and read the short message to decide whether it’s a syntax issue, an undeclared identifier, or a linker undefined reference. A recommended practice is to fix errors top-to-bottom because one error can cascade additional messages. As a guided task, introduce a missing semicolon intentionally, recompile, read the message, and then fix it to see the edit-compile-run loop in action. What sequence will you follow when the compiler reports three errors at once?

keyIdea.title: Fix order
keyIdea.text: Read messages top-to-bottom; fix the first error, then recompile to avoid chasing spurious downstream errors.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Common Errors
Missing semicolon
Compiler points to a syntax error near the line. Fix by adding the missing semicolon at statement end.
Wrong case for main()
main must be lowercase. Using Main or MAIN can prevent the program from starting correctly.
Missing include for iostream
If std::cout is undeclared, add #include <iostream> at the top. The compiler will then recognize the symbol.
Guided example
Introduce a missing semicolon in your main.cpp, compile, and read the message. The compiler often shows the next line and a caret that indicates where it detected the problem. Fixing that first often resolves additional errors that were caused by the missing punctuation.
Warning

Do not ignore the first error in the list. Fix it and recompile before addressing later messages.

screens.title: Recommended Beginner Environment
screens.narratorSegment: For this course we recommend an accessible, cross-platform setup that is friendly for beginners. On Windows many learners use Visual Studio Code as a lightweight editor and install the MinGW-w64 toolchain to obtain g++. On Mac O S and Linux, the system-provided GCC or Clang toolchains are common and work well. The IDE supplies a comfortable editor, extensions for C++, and an integrated terminal where you can run the compiler. Practical steps include installing V S Code, adding the C/C++ extension so you get syntax highlighting and basic debugging assistance, and confirming you can run g++ from the terminal. A typical check is opening a terminal inside your project directory, creating main. cpp, compiling with g++ main. cpp -o mygame, and running the produced executable. If g++ is not on PATH the terminal will say the command is not found — that indicates a missing or misconfigured compiler. The setup described here keeps your environment simple while preparing you to integrate more advanced tools or engines later. Which platform will you set up first, and can you confirm g++ is reachable from the terminal?

screens.title: Common Setup Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Three setup pitfalls often slow beginners: the compiler not being on PATH, trying to run source files directly, and misinterpreting compiler output. If g++ is not found, the terminal will report that the command is missing; this usually means the compiler was not installed or PATH was not updated. Fixing PATH is a configuration step outside the compiler. Another mistake is trying to execute main. cpp directly; source files are not runnable — you must compile to produce an executable and then run that executable. Misreading messages is also common: compilation and linking errors come from different phases and require different fixes. For example, a message saying undefined reference indicates a linker problem, not a syntax mistake. To avoid confusion, run the compiler command and read the topmost error first, then correct it and recompile. Practicing these checks during the activity will make them habitual. After this, you’ll spend less time on tooling and more time building game systems. Which of these pitfalls surprised you most during setup? Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Pitfalls
Compiler not found
Terminal says command not found. This is a PATH or installation problem. Confirm installation and add the compiler folder to your system PATH.
Running source instead of executable
You must compile source files into an executable before running. Executing main.cpp directly will not work because it's not machine code.
Misreading errors
Differentiate compiler errors from linker errors. Fix syntax issues first, then address undefined references that appear during linking.

screens.title: Entry Point and Headers
screens.narratorSegment: Two central language elements every program must use are header inclusion and the main function. Headers like iostream provide declarations that let the compiler know what std::cout and std::endl mean; without including the header the compiler will report undeclared identifiers. The main function is the program's entry point; its typical signature is int main() and it should return an integer. Returning zero is the conventional way to signal success to the operating system, while returning non-zero indicates an error condition. A common beginner confusion is thinking main can be any name or case—main is special and must be lowercase. Another misunderstanding is forgetting that including a header does not automatically compile library code; it only provides declarations. Linking provides the actual library implementations. When you write small programs, include only the headers you need and keep main small so it remains easy to test and evolve. A good habit is to place initialization code in clearly named functions and call them from main, which improves readability as projects grow. How might you structure a small game loop so main remains a simple coordinator?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will build the minimal, reliable workspace that lets C++ code become a runnable program. We’ll clarify two essential roles: the compiler, which translates your human-readable code into machine instructions, and the IDE, which organizes your files and runs the compiler for you. You will see a short terminal-style demo that compiles a simple greeting program and we’ll intentionally create a couple of common mistakes so you learn to read compiler messages. This foundation matters because game development relies on fast, predictable builds and confident debugging. By the end you’ll have a working main. cpp, know how to compile it with g++ or the MinGW toolchain on Windows, and be comfortable locating and fixing the typical errors beginners make. Along the way I’ll show why header inclusion like iostream is required, what main() must look like, and how the linker produces the final executable. Let’s begin by mapping the tools, then we’ll create your first program and run it so you know your environment is ready.

By the end of this lesson you will perform four concrete skills vital to starting game development in C++. First, you will explain the roles of an IDE and a compiler in plain language and know why each tool is necessary for building executables. Second, you will set up a basic development environment suitable for beginners: Visual Studio Code with MinGW on Windows, or GCC/Clang on Mac O S and Linux. Third, you will write, compile, and execute a simple console program that prints a friendly message; this validates your toolchain and proves you can go from source to executable. Fourth, you will identify and correct common early compilation errors, like forgetting semicolons or using the wrong capitalization for main, and you will read error lines to locate the problem. Each objective includes practice you can perform immediately so you gain confidence. These skills ensure that when you later add libraries or game engines, your foundation remains solid and you can focus on gameplay rather than toolchain problems.

These objectives emphasize doing as much as understanding. You will perform short checks: install and launch your editor, open a terminal, and run a compile command. For Windows learners we recommend configuring the MinGW-w64 toolchain so the g++ command is available in PATH; Mac O S and Linux typically provide GCC or Clang. You will write two small console outputs inside main. cpp to confirm sequential execution and observe flushing behavior when using the newline manipulator. When you intentionally introduce an error such as removing a semicolon or capitalizing Main, you will read the compiler's message and correct the line. This practice is essential because reading and acting on compiler feedback is one of the most powerful developer skills. These short tasks make the environment tangible and reproducible, so later you can focus on game systems rather than installation problems.

C++ is a common choice for high-performance games because it gives programmers direct control over memory and an efficient path to machine instructions. In practice this means game systems like physics, rendering, and audio can be written to use memory deterministically and avoid unnecessary copies. For you as a beginner, that translates into code that can run faster and integrate tightly with game engines. A concrete example: a collision system that iterates millions of objects per frame benefits from C++ performance and predictable allocation. A common misconception is that C++ is only for experts; while it has powerful features, you can start with a small subset—basic functions, simple data structures, and clear ownership rules—before using advanced features. Another contrast: higher-level languages trade some speed for safety and easier syntax, which is fine for tools or rapid prototypes. The takeaway is to start with readable, well-structured C++ and focus on learning compilation and debugging before optimizing. That foundation lets you later adopt engine-specific systems with confidence. How might knowing memory behavior change how you design a game loop? Why C++ is used for Game Development means c++ provides the performance and control needed for game engines; begin with simple constructs and learn the compile-run cycle first.. In practical terms, performance, memory control, and hardware access explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the distinct roles of compiler, linker, and IDE prevents confusion when builds fail. The compiler reads your C++ source files, checks syntax, applies preprocessing directives, and generates object code. Think of it as translating your recipe into machine fragments. The linker then takes those object files plus necessary library code and combines them into a single executable your OS can run. Without the linker, separate object files remain isolated pieces. An IDE is the environment that helps you edit files, run the compiler and linker, and debug. For example, Visual Studio Code running a terminal command like g++ main. cpp -o mygame. exe automates invoking the compiler and then the produced binary can be run. A common beginner mistake is trying to run source files directly instead of the compiled executable; the compiler must be present and reachable in PATH. Another mistake is ignoring linker errors that indicate missing functions from other object files or libraries. Fixing these means confirming compilation succeeds for all translation units and linking required libraries. How will you check whether compilation or linking failed next time you see an error?

Now we will study a minimal C++ program that prints a greeting. This example uses the standard input-output header and a main function that returns zero to indicate success. Read the code first, then I will explain each part and why it is required. Notice the preprocessor directive that includes iostream and the use of the std::cout object with the insertion operator to send text to the console. The endl manipulator inserts a newline and flushes output so you see the message immediately. A common beginner error is omitting the semicolon at the end of the output line; that produces a syntax error during compilation. Another is writing Main or MAIN instead of main—the entry point must be lowercase. Use this sample as your first file named main. cpp. After you type it, save and compile. The code is compact and portable across platforms if you have a working toolchain. What output do you expect when this runs, and what would a missing semicolon error look like in the compiler output? Your First C++ Program means include iostream, define int main, output via std::cout, end with return 0; to signal successful execution.. In practical terms, a readable walkthrough of the hello message program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Compiling C++ is a multi-step process that transforms source files into an executable. First, the preprocessor handles directives like include; it inserts header contents so the compiler sees declarations. Next, the compiler proper parses and type-checks the code, reporting syntax and semantic errors and producing assembly or object code. After that an assembler converts assembly to machine-level object files. Finally, the linker resolves references across object files and libraries and produces the final executable file that the operating system can run. A concrete example: when you run g++ main. cpp -o mygame. exe, the toolchain performs these phases, often in one command. Beginners often confuse which phase reported an error. If you see a syntax error mentioning a line in your source, that’s from the compiler phase. If you see undefined reference errors during linking, the compiler produced object code but the linker could not find needed functions in the linked objects or libraries. Practice reading which phase produced the message so you know whether to edit source, add a missing object file, or include a library. What change would you make if the linker reports an undefined reference to a function you implemented in another file?
